title: How 46 fashion designers reimagined McLaren’s F1 history
excerpt:
On Wednesday evening, the McLaren Technology Centre looked markedly different having been transformed into a fashion runway.

Instead of team personnel, it was models walking between some of McLaren's most famous cars that took centre stage, wearing a very different interpretation of the team’s history.

This was Designed to Race: Front Row, a show where 46 MA fashion students from Central Saint Martins presented 12 looks inspired by more than six decades of McLaren history.

James Hunt’s approach to racewear was one of the clearest references in the collection. So was the yellow of Ayrton Senna’s helmet, old racing equipment, engineering drawings and, much later in the collection, the papaya-clad fan culture surrounding the team today.

However, unlike many fashion collaborations, the students were not designing something for McLaren to sell.

“I think this was really about opening up a conversation,” McLaren Racing Chief Marketing Officer Louise McEwen exclusively told F1.com after the show. “The more we worked together, the more we realised, although we are in different spheres and different businesses, how similar we were.

“Both are incredible high-performing teams coming together with incredible craft, creativity and ingenuity at the heart of everything that we do. So it’s been a brilliant journey with them over the last nine months or so, coming up with the collections and working with the team there.”

The students had been split into 12 groups and handed a wide brief. A driver or famous car could be the starting point, but so could a period in McLaren’s history, the engineering behind the team or the people around it.

The finished collection moved through five chapters: Grit x Glamour, Precision and Power, Global Icon, Engineered Athlete and Papaya Era.

From the 1970s to Senna

The collection begins with the 1970s, when McLaren were establishing themselves as one of Formula 1’s leading teams.

Emerson Fittipaldi delivered McLaren’s first Drivers’ Championship in 1974, the same year they won their first Constructors’ Championship. Away from the results, F1 was changing too. Television audiences were growing and drivers were becoming increasingly recognisable away from the track.

James Hunt arrived at McLaren shortly afterwards and his unique style gave the students plenty to work with.

His habit of wearing his overalls tied around his waist, his disregard for formal dress and his wider image fed into Grit x Glamour. Flared silhouettes, leather, orange tones and distressed finishes all appeared, taking elements of Hunt’s style without simply recreating his wardrobe.

Speaking during a panel discussion ahead of the show, Central Saint Martins MA Fashion Course Leader Fabio Piras explained that the brief deliberately left room for that kind of interpretation.

“The brief was interesting because it wasn’t asking us to necessarily design a piece of fashion, an outfit," he said. "It was an interpretation of a period, of an era, of a character, of obviously an iconic champion and a car.

“I think the visit of the students to the Technology Centre was an absolutely bombastic moment for them, because actually you don’t realise how fantastic those cars are if you don’t see them closely, even in terms of design objects. They’re amazing design objects.”

For MA Fashion student Enzo Keuning, that freedom was what made the project interesting.

“What made this project unique was that there wasn’t one way to interpret that heritage. Each group brought a different perspective, from engineering and performance, to identity and craftsmanship, and we were challenged to transform those ideas into something new.

“My background in econometrics has taught me to look at systems through patterns, relationships and connections, so I found it fascinating to approach McLaren’s history through fashion.”

As the collection moved through McLaren’s history, some of the references became more technical. Senna’s famous yellow helmet was one of the clearest, but the students also looked at his precise driving style and the idea of speed. The resulting pieces used lightweight fabrics, shapes informed by airflow and digitally developed patterns.

Other groups looked away from the driver completely. One design centred on a female fire marshal, while track layouts, old team graphics and pieces of racing equipment appeared in smaller details throughout the collection.

Sometimes you had to look twice. Monaco’s famous hairpin, for example, was stitched inside a pair of trousers.

The details behind the clothes

Getting those 12 looks to the runway took months.

Fashion, Piras told the panel, is usually seen at the point where the work is already done. The audience gets the runway, but not the months of changing ideas, criticism and mistakes that came before it.

“When we see fashion, we always see the outcome. We see the 10-minute performance at the end. That’s the length of a fashion show.

“What an audience doesn’t have access to is the time it takes to get to those 10 outfits, in this case 12. The process of fashion is trial and error.

"You build the narrative, you build the information that will inform your fashion, but then it’s about trying things out and moving on with the mistakes. That’s how you create fashion.”

Piras’ description of trial and error was familiar territory for McLaren too, even if the measurements involved look very different.

During the panel, McEwen recalled how small the margins can become, using a request to save weight ahead of the 2025 British Grand Prix as an example.

“As a team, we’re in a constant state, similarly to Central Saint Martins, of reinvention. We have a saying that we absolutely can’t stand still because we have to keep innovating to stay at the front of the grid. If we don’t, we’re definitely going backwards.

“Even at the front, it boils down to microns and milliseconds that can make the difference between those grid positions for us.

“Last year, going into the British Grand Prix, our Team Principal said, ‘Lou, we need to save weight,’ and I can’t tell you how much, but it’s fair to say it was some segments of papaya that really make the difference. That’s the precision and detailing, and I think it was really evident working through the design process how much of that came through in the students’ designs.”

Engineering blueprints and aerodynamic forms fed into patterns and silhouettes, while carbon fibre and upcycled racing seatbelts were brought into the collection itself, with fabric offcuts, second-hand materials and used McLaren equipment also appearing across the 12 looks.

The Papaya era

Jump forward five decades and the references become perhaps easier to recognise.

Papaya dominates, racewear is mixed with denim and knitwear, and even Daniel Ricciardo’s ‘Shoey’ makes an appearance as a headpiece.

The final chapter looked at the current McLaren era and the audience surrounding it. One group played with the idea of young fans seeing drivers as heroes, using toy cars, childlike drawings and a cape-like silhouette, while used McLaren racing boots from previous eras were brought back for the finished look.

The way fans interact with Formula 1 now was one of the reasons McLaren wanted to do the project in the first place.

During the panel, F1 Presenter Ariana Bravo spoke about just how much the audience around the sport has changed.

“Formula 1 has seen a growth in its audience in a way that I don’t think any of us within the sport were expecting," she said. "It’s a much younger and a much more diverse audience now.

“With that comes a different way that people want to consume our sport. It’s not just about watching the cars go around on track anymore. It’s about everything that surrounds that as well.

“Yes, of course, they’re fans of the racing first and foremost, but they also want to tap into the culture. They want to tap into the lifestyle aspect of it. They don’t want to just tap into the drivers in race mode. They want to have this accessibility 24/7, and they want to be able to express their support for a team through fashion, through culture.”

McEwen told F1.com that Global F1 Fan data shows nearly half of fans consider fashion important to the way they express their fandom. That data helped inform the project, although McEwen says success cannot simply be measured in reach or engagement.

“We are obsessed by data, and the whole piece tonight was informed by data," she said. "The fact that our fans, and half of F1 fans broadly, actually say that fashion is important to them and it’s how they show their fandom.

“But everything that you saw today was very much about creativity and humanness coming through.

“In terms of measurement, I think it’s a blend. It’s not one or the other. Tonight we opened the doors to the McLaren Technology Centre to many in the media who had never been here before, probably seeing a different side of us and our sport.

“Hopefully that will reach many new fans who might have been thinking about Formula 1, might not know anything about Formula 1, but might be fashion lovers, and vice versa. I think it’s just about that crossover between popular culture and sport that we’re seeing so much of right now.”

That changing audience was visible off the runway too, with guests from across motorsport, fashion, music and sport inside the McLaren Technology Centre for the show.

McLaren team mates Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri were joined by F1 ACADEMY drivers Ella Lloyd and Ella Stevens, as well as Freddie Hunt, son of James.

But also in attendance were models Mia Regan, Amechi Madu and Denola Gray, rapper Kojey Radical and Olympic medallist Amy Hunt.

McLaren are far from alone in embracing fashion, but McEwen is wary of suggesting any team can assume they have already worked out what this newer audience wants.

“I think in this game, you can never think you’re ahead of the curve, right?" she added. "There’s always someone just behind you waiting to catch up.

“I like to think that, as a team, we’ve really driven innovation in this space. Tonight again, I think we’ve shown another side of us. Showing up in a space where performance meets culture with that authenticity has been really important to us, and establishing a relationship with Central Saint Martins.”

For McEwen, giving creatives the freedom to interpret McLaren in their own way was also central to the project, and something she believes is just as important away from the track.

“We have to be as competitive off the grid as we are on it, and I think the point is, without creativity, we’re never going to appeal to new fans, we’re never going to have new ideas, and I think you’ve got to be really careful not to stifle that creativity.

“Tonight, you can see what can happen when you give people a little bit of inspiration, but then give them that scope to go and design and see where they want to go.

“I didn’t know quite what we were going to get tonight, and I’m just blown away and super excited.”

title: Why Williams' FW48 upgrade package in Baku is so crucial
excerpt:
The Azerbaijan Grand Prix will be a huge weekend for the Williams team as they finally introduce the long-awaited major upgrade package for the FW48.

Up until now the 2026 season has been a painful one for drivers Carlos Sainz and Alex Albon, especially in the light of the promise shown last year.

Delays forced the team to miss the Barcelona Shakedown, and when it finally took to the track the car proved to be significantly overweight, as well as having some inherent issues.

At an early stage, much like Aston Martin, the team took the decision to focus on a major package for the second half of the season, although in the case of Williams some new bits have been introduced along the way, such as a revised front wing for Silverstone. There has also been an ongoing programme of trimming weight.

However, the results tell their own story. In the early races the drivers managed to log five points finishes, with a best of P8 for Albon in the high attrition Monaco Grand Prix. However, since then the team have failed to score a single point, with the cars typically finishing in the P15, P16 and P17 range.

In part that’s down to an improved reliability record across the field since the early races, but it also reflects the fact that rivals have been improving while Williams have made little progress.

“I think what's been interesting this year is most of the midfield teams, they always bring one or two upgrades a year,” Albon noted after a difficult race in Madrid last weekend. “That's kind of how it's gone. This year, even the midfield teams are bringing three or four upgrades a year, and the size of upgrades are huge as well.

“So if you think of us in a normal year, Baku would have put us back in contention. But we have to be honest with ourselves, the speed of the development race this year is huge – and yeah, we've fallen back.”

In other words, when the Baku package was signed off several months ago the numbers looked promising in terms of the potential gains. However, as other midfield cars have improved, the goalposts have moved.

The FW48 will be faster, there’s little doubt – but it’s all relative, and there might not be the dramatic surge up the grid that may have originally seemed possible.

It is also likely to be the last roll of the dice for Williams in 2026, as the focus turns increasingly to next season and the FW50.

“We're finishing realistically 50 seconds behind the midfield at the minute in a race,” said Albon. “So we're losing a second a lap, more or less, in the race, and this has to be a pretty big upgrade to do it. Let's see.

“We know it's going to be a good step. Is it going to be the full step? I'm hopeful for it, but I don't think it will be. Unfortunately, we said it last year, but the focus is on next year as well. And we realise we're too far back at the moment to have a couple of upgrades for this year. We need to focus on next year.”

Last year Sainz qualified second and finished third in Azerbaijan, a reminder of just how competitive Williams were at some venues. Like Albon, the Spaniard is keeping his expectations in check.

“I think that upgrade is going to definitely help us to get ourselves closer to potentially fighting for some points,” he said at his home race. “But realistically speaking, that’s nowhere near where we wanted to be this year, nowhere near what we promised. So, it’s still not enough, and it’s still not where we want to be.

How Sainz's home race in Madrid unravelled

“It’s an upgrade that will help a bit the motivation of the team and just to look into the weekend with something to look forward to, maybe to potentially get a point or two when we were like we were at the beginning of the year.

“But it’s nowhere near where we want to be, and I think our biggest hope is putting all the eggs in next year’s basket.”

Sainz makes a good point about motivation. The Baku package might not allow the team to move into contention for Q3, but the important thing is that it brings the performance gains that were calculated months ago.

That would be a demonstration that the processes are working, and will also give the design team the confidence that they are going in the right direction with the FW50.

Baku is thus crucial for Team Principal James Vowles, the man tasked with taking Williams back to title contention, and who a few weeks ago convinced Albon and Sainz to commit for the future.

Vowles highlighted changes in processes and methodology and a wave of key recruits (such as Chief Optimisation and Planning Officer Piers Thynne) as reasons for the drivers to have faith that the team won’t make the same mistakes that they made ahead of 2026.

“You're making a thousand decisions in the winter,” Vowles noted at Zandvoort. “You don't need many of them to be wrong before you start putting yourself into the wrong path. And that'll be the difference between a few tenths, but a few tenths these days is the between winning a championship or not.

“You go to the level of what are the big building blocks you're putting in place? Which is a combination of people, which is different to what we had before. A combination of strength in the team that was different to what we had before.

“And for us, we had a lack last year at the beginning of '25 of simulation technology. That actually only came online in November last year. The car was already pretty much done by that point in time.

“So what we were doing was using educated guessing, and we got some of it wrong. If you look at our rear ride height, we developed at the wrong rear ride height, as did Aston, for that matter, and corrected it.

“That doesn't seem like a huge amount. But you're aerodynamically developing in completely the wrong space, and it's not driven by anything more than simulation telling you that's a good direction for whatever characteristic you're after, and it goes wrong.

“That error can still be made across any winter, because you're in a theoretical space against a maximal space.”

If it does what it’s supposed to do, the Baku package will be a sign that things are moving in the right direction at Grove.

However, Vowles makes no guarantees that there won’t be some missteps with the development of the 2027 car: “Not for a second am I going to promise anyone, because there's no championship team that would.

“What you're more trying to do is show that there's enough depth that didn't exist previously in the ways of working systems, tools, processes, and people that allow you to catch as many of those as possible.”

title: Inside the Italian dinner party staged on Monza's grid
excerpt:
The world of Formula 1 is passionate, high-energy and non-stop, so the opportunity to truly slow down and take it all in is one that shouldn’t be passed up. Barilla recognised the unique chance to do just that in a short moment of peace ahead of the Italian Grand Prix.

A fortunate group made up of drivers both past and present, team members, journalists and fans were invited to enjoy an exquisite three-course meal cooked by Michelin-starred chef Massimo Bottura, who admitted that the prospect of cooking pasta perfectly al dente for hundreds of people was a somewhat daunting task.

Before the time for that came, I ventured down the eerily quiet pit lane – usually a place punctuated by the noise of wheel guns and hubbub of mechanics – to the grid entrance, where Barilla representatives handed over a pass labelled ‘La Tavolata’ and a much-needed handheld fan.

We were well into the evening hours, but the tarmac insistently emitted the heat it had absorbed through the day, so I was more than grateful for the token. It was similarly branded with the event name – an Italian term for a large crowd sharing a meal at a single, shared table.

And that was exactly what filled the starting grid. I couldn’t help but take in the enormity of the long table, draped in a white cloth with accents of dark blue, while wine glasses sparkled in the last of the sun’s light. The grandstands were empty, but a Ferrari flag acted as a reminder of the action to come.

The chatter of this F1 microcosm grew louder as I headed towards the iconic five red lights, where small tables were surrounded by stalls offering bruschetta, cured meat, cheese, champagne and breadsticks, all covered by canopies in the same white and blue colourway.

A roaming band made up of four players flexed their talents with crowd-pleasers by The Beatles, visiting each huddle of attendees in turn and making it practically impossible to avoid smiling – even more so when they switched to irresistible Italian classics like Mambo Italiano and Sarà Perché Ti Amo.

From Ascari to Antonelli – Monza’s most magical home wins

After I consumed a borderline embarrassing number of hors d’oeuvres, we were directed to take our seats and inspect the menu. For someone who adores both F1 and food, this experience was my equivalent of a dog hearing the words ‘walk’ or ‘treat’.

Barilla pasta, pesto, dessert, Monza, starting grid… it was getting pretty hard to hide my excitement, and I was far from alone – everyone had a look in their eyes that conveyed an appreciative disbelief at the whole evening.

First up was Fusilloni Al Bronzo al Pesto, which the menu described as a “reinterpretation of traditional Ligurian pesto” with a pea cream and toasted breadcrumbs, creating a “testimony to extraordinary flavours”.

“I'm a little bit stressed because I'm thinking about 35 kilos of pasta that has to come out al dente at least – it's not easy and my hands are sweating,” Bottura conceded in his welcome speech. “I feel a little butterfly in my stomach, but okay, it’s part of the challenge so I'll do it.

“This is exactly the example of the classic Italian Tavolata. You know, we sit together, we share together. This is Italian cuisine and this is the reason because the Italian cuisine has been named UNESCO Heritage. It's not because Italian cuisine is one cuisine. There are 100,000 cuisines in Italy.

“It's their ritual of sitting around the table, sharing a meal in a refectory or in a three Michelin star restaurant. It's the same. Cooking is an act of love, that's it. And when you do it, you do it for your friends, for your family, or for the F1 family.”

He went on to outline the fresh, aromatic herbs that blended together to make the most vibrant green pesto I’ve ever seen, marking the first of two dishes to showcase Barilla pasta. The next was the main course – affectionately titled ‘Lap Two’ to tie in further with our location.

Barilla went above and beyond in their role as an F1 Official Partner by making a limited edition pasta called Gran Ruote. Inspired by the shape of wheels, its spokes are perfectly placed to capture all the sauce, which in this case was a delightfully simple cacio e pepe made from Parmigiano Reggiano and pepper.

Last up was the final lap of the meal: ‘L’essenza del Sole Siciliano’. Bottura described this creation as “a beautiful idea of the power of the sun, of the beauty of Italy”.

Michelin-starred chef Massimo Bottura reveals his F1 heroes

“For me, when I think about Italy and I think of the sun, I think Sicily,” he explained. “The whole dessert is like the power of Sicily with all the citrus and almonds and capers and coffee and the fruit of Sicily.”

It was a refreshing conclusion to a night in which I like to think I achieved the aim of La Tavolata – sharing conversations with those from all walks of F1 and coming together to bask in a community unlike any other. Paolo Barilla, a former racer himself, summarised that feeling well with a story from his childhood.

“In 1974 I was there [indicating a nearby grandstand],” he relayed to the crowd of diners. “I wanted to see Formula 1 from very close, but it was far. Two Ferraris were leading – Clay Regazzoni and Niki Lauda – and both of them retired.

“I was 13 years old. I was desperate. Disaster! My first Grand Prix, my heart beating for Ferrari and I see two Ferraris stop at the beginning of the pit lane. In 1975, Ferrari got first place with Clay Regazzoni and third place with Niki and they won the championship.

“And then I go to 1980, when I made the first lap with Formula Fiat Abarth here. Going there to the first chicane, I felt the immensity of this place, the history on my shoulders, and I was amazed by the emotion I felt. I would say that Monza, between the highs and lows, it's an emotional place.

“To have all of you here around the table where we want the people to get together, share the emotion, and then on Sunday they have to fight. The fight is a part of life, but the friendship around the table is very important.”

title: Football legend José Mourinho on his love for F1
excerpt:
Two worlds came together at last weekend’s Spanish Grand Prix when legendary football coach – and long-time F1 fan – José Mourinho paid a visit to the Madring circuit to follow the action.

Ahead of Sunday’s race, which took place just a stone’s throw away from Real Madrid’s training ground, F1.com grabbed a few words with the Portuguese tactician to discuss the Spanish capital’s all-new Grand Prix, his passion for racing, and how F1 compares (and differs) to football…

It’s Saturday night in Madrid and the streets are buzzing with Real fans who, after watching their team beat Inter Milan 2-1 in the Champions League mid-week, expect more of the same from a La Liga fixture against Rayo Vallecano.

Once inside the 83,000-capacity Bernabéu stadium, Mourinho and his group of star players waste no time in putting on a show – Los Blancos racing into a 3-0 lead by half-time with goals from the likes of Kylian Mbappé and Jude Bellingham. By the end of the game, a commanding 4-1 scoreline brings them level on points with rivals FC Barcelona at the top of the table.

Some 12 hours later, after a well-earned rest, Mourinho, Bellingham and other team members have swapped that hallowed turf for new ground in the form of the Madring – F1’s hybrid street/permanent circuit built around the IFEMA Exhibition Centre, and less than four kilometres from Madrid’s training pitches.

Mourinho is no stranger to the F1 paddock, having made several visits in previous seasons, including last year’s British Grand Prix, but there is something particularly meaningful for him this time around.

“I’ve enjoyed it [F1] for a while, and I’ve been to a few races, but of course this is the first one [at the Madring],” Mourinho tells F1.com.

“Because I work just around the corner, every day that I was coming to work or leaving work, I was following it, the building [process], and the more we were approaching this day, [there was] more emotion for everybody.”

Given that Mourinho has gone from the football field to the F1 grid on multiple occasions, it begs an obvious question: what do the two sports have in common, and how are they different?

For the 63-year-old, who has also managed Manchester United, Inter Milan, Chelsea and Roma, among other clubs, there is a standout common theme – as well as an area in which he feels football can learn from F1.

“You know, it’s huge pressure for both,” he says thoughtfully. “When you have sports at the highest level, we are always speaking about huge pressure.

“But I feel that they [F1] are one step ahead of us in terms of the way they approach the big moments. [In football] we close each other [off], I believe, too much, also because of tradition.

“These guys [the drivers], [there’s] huge pressure, but before that [time in the car], they are together, they meet people, they do a little bit of PR, they do a little bit of media.

“I think we have to learn with them, the way they can be relaxed, and half an hour later they can be in the car fighting for their lives, because they take risks.”

Since his first managerial stint with Portuguese club Benfica back in 2000, Mourinho has racked up more than 25 major trophies – the UEFA Champions League, the UEFA Cup/Europa League, the Premier League, the FA Cup, other national titles and plenty more, along with a host of individual accolades.

However, what about the hypothetical challenge of leaving football behind and becoming an F1 team boss?

“I have no idea!” Mourinho responds, with his eyes widening at the prospect. “I just have to learn. I learn with [F1 President and CEO] Stefano Domenicali; I ask him lots of questions. I tried to learn with all of them [the people I meet], and I like very much to come [to watch F1].

“It was not possible [on Saturday], because I had a match day, but I like to come for the Qualifyings, I like to come for the training sessions [Free Practices], because then clearly you can be closer, and you can interact more.

“Today is their day, and it’s the day I like to respect their privacy.”

Nonetheless, Mourinho has met and struck up friendships with many F1 drivers and personalities since experiencing the sport for the first time – his tour of the Madring on Sunday still featuring various catch-ups and motorhome visits.

That included conversations with the aforementioned Domenicali, and four-time World Champion Max Verstappen, who was presented with his pole position award by Mourinho at Silverstone in 2025.

“I know almost all of them, and everybody [has been] so nice to me over so many years,” Mourinho continues. “Now we’re coming to some new people, to some new generations, but I always had great respect from them.

“Because, as a family, we are so close to Stefano, it is of course a great way to be invited – we invited ourselves! – and to have always the reception that we have.”

Mourinho’s latest visit might have been a fleeting one, but judging by his comments above, there is no doubt that one of football’s most iconic figures will be back for more in the future.

title: Mekies offers update on Hadjar's injury recovery
excerpt:
Isack Hadjar has missed the three races since the summer break ended, sitting out Zandvoort, Monza and Madrid as he recovers from an injury sustained in training. The Frenchman hurt his wrist in the three-week break, and has been on the sidelines ever since.

In his absence, Liam Lawson has stepped up into the vacant Red Bull seat, with Yuki Tsunoda filling Lawson’s cockpit at Racing Bulls.

Those two have done an admirable job in difficult circumstances, but they face a wait to see just who will be where for the next Grand Prix in Azerbaijan.

Red Bull team boss Laurent Mekies clarified the situation in the wake of the Spanish Grand Prix, confirming that there had been no additional setbacks for Hadjar, and that his recovery was taking as long as expected.

“Isack is good... There is nothing wrong with Isack's recovery. I think we have learned that it's fundamentally normal time for the sort of injuries he has,” Mekies said.

“So, we will continue with the same approach than what we had, we will evaluate the situations in a weeks’ time, we have a full week, with more than a full week to evaluate the situation to see how he feels.

“And then to put him on the simulator, to expose him to real-life constraints… If he feels close to 100%, we go for it. If he feels the recovery is not completed, we will stick [with] our approach to put his recovery first.

“What we don't want to do is by having an early return, compromise his long-term capacity to come back to 100%.”

Hadjar has made a strong start to his time with Red Bull, with eight top-10 finishes, including a podium in Monaco. He has also managed to out-qualify Max Verstappen three times.

This injury setback is far from ideal, with the Frenchman having missed out not just on points, but on learning more about the RB22 as everyone continues to get to grips with the new generation of cars.

He has still attended races and thus will have been looking at the data, but that is not the same as driving and understanding exactly where the latest upgrades are taking the car.

In his absence, Verstappen has taken two podiums to show what the car is capable of, while Lawson has finished in the points twice from his three drives with the team.

Another driver in recent memory to come back from a wrist injury was Lance Stroll, who had a bicycle accident prior to the start of the season in 2023. He missed testing but drove in the opening race and scored points despite having a broken wrist and toe.

Daniel Ricciardo was out considerably longer than Stroll when he broke a bone in his hand in 2023 after crashing in practice at Zandvoort. The Australian wound up missing five Grands Prix – with Lawson being his replacement at the time.

It seems that Red Bull are happy to leave it late to make a call on whether Hadjar will return to the cockpit for the upcoming triple header, or whether he will remain on the sidelines for the time being.

title: 'Bit of a shock to the system' leading Cadillac – Budkowski
excerpt:
Marcin Budkowski admits that returning to Formula 1 has been "a bit of a shock to the system", having been put in charge of the Cadillac team.

The Pole has been with the American team for nearly a month, having replaced Graeme Lowdon as Team Principal just before the Dutch Grand Prix at the end of August.

Budkowski is no stranger to F1, having worked with multiple championship-winning Formula 1 teams across sporting and technical divisions and within senior leadership teams, including Prost, McLaren, Alpine and the FIA.

Having left the sport in 2022, Budkowski found himself in a new role with media organisations Eleven Sports Poland and Viaplay, before the call from Cadillac.

Ahead of last weekend's Spanish Grand Prix, Budkowski admitted that the return to a prominent role in the sport had been a bit of a shock.

"What hits you first is the pace of F1, which I knew well but a few years out of the sport and it's a bit of a shock to the system because it's incredibly fast-paced, technical and hard-working, especially when you start in a new team and new project," said Budkowski during Friday's teams' press conference.

"The other thing is the first time I sat again on the pit wall in FP1 in Zandvoort and I had 12 channels blasting in my ears. It took me a little bit of time for my brain to get used to it.

"But the reality is, if you bring it back to the essentials and basics, it's about people, it's about building the team. It's about putting the right people in the right positions, getting everybody to work together and in terms of leadership, give them a vision and align everybody in that direction. That hasn't changed."

Cadillac have endured a difficult maiden season in F1 so far, remaining the only team on the grid yet to score a point, with Valtteri Bottas' P13 in the Chinese Grand Prix the team's best result to date.

Despite the lack of pace and reliability so far, Budkowski has been encouraged by what he has seen, despite having been at the helm for only three races.

"I've seen a lot of good things in the team, and it's pretty impressive given the time they had to build the team and conditions with the entry and everything.

"A lot of good things, there's no legacy compared to some other teams. There's a lot of open-minded, constructive discussions going on but there's also a number of shortcuts that are being taken, which is inevitable when you build a new team in such a time.

"It's about working in some areas that need more attention. In the short-term, reliability. We've seen we've struggled with that in some areas and just getting the operational excellence to the next level, which is not the level of a top team as of today, but that's understandable.

"Longer term, there's some clearer priorities emerging for what we need to do and better, mostly to improve our performance and our pace."

title: Tsunoda reveals his biggest mistake at Red Bull in 2025
excerpt:
Yuki Tsunoda has enjoyed a surprise three race cameo in 2026, slotting into Racing Bulls in place of Liam Lawson following Isack Hadjar’s injury. While it remains unknown whether Tsunoda will get a fourth outing this season, the Japanese racer has certainly made the most of his unexpected comeback.

Tsunoda is Red Bull’s reserve driver this season, having lost his race seat at the end of last year. After being promoted to Red Bull from the third round of the 2025 season, Tsunoda struggled to make much of an impact and was resigned to playing a support role in Max Verstappen’s championship bid.

Speaking on the latest episode of official F1 podcast Beyond the Grid, Tsunoda explained just how tough 2025 was for him, after many years of relative success at Racing Bulls under their various guises, and exactly what he felt was his biggest mistake.

“One thing about myself I think, if I say [being] completely honest, I have a big enough ego to not change my driving style,” Tsunoda said. “I know what I'm doing in terms of driving. I believe in myself, so I never try to change my driving style to other drivers, even though the driver is competitive and fast.

“Obviously Max, it's a different case, he's a World Champion, he proves a lot of things and I still learn a lot of things from his driving. [It was] probably the first year out of any years since I started that I thought about changing driving style and tried to do something similar to Max.

“But in my perspective, if I just look at data, I didn't really see a huge difference in terms of driving. What I think now is the biggest mistake in last year was to try to replicate the set-up what he's doing.”

Tsunoda scored just seven times out of the 21 Grands Prix he contested with Red Bull, in a car that Verstappen took to second in the championship. The comparison between the two late in that season was stark, with Verstappen winning five of the final eight races, while Tsunoda in the same period recorded a P6, P7 and P10 finish.

That resulted in Tsunoda losing his seat, with Hadjar promoted from Racing Bulls to replace him.

“When I got told, I still remember, I didn't feel that much of huge disappointment or devastated feeling. Obviously, still disappointed and pretty sad that I'm not driving next year. But not as I expected, I don't know why.

“I fought really hard. I fought more than ever in that 2025 year, more than ever. And even if I look back now, I don't have much regret. I gave everything and the outcome is something I didn't like, obviously, but honestly, I just gave everything.”

Tsunoda believes the struggles he went through in 2025 have made him a better driver, and he has impressed for Racing Bulls.

In a new generation of cars, which are very different from what he drove last year, Tsunoda has done well in the three races he has contested – especially in Zandvoort, where the Sprint format meant he only had one practice session to get used to all the changes.

The issue Red Bull are still trying to correct on the RB22

“Going back to this Netherlands story, jumping into the car that I’ve never driven, Sprint Qualifying format, team is doing really well, you know, running P5 in Championship, [knowing] that you can't really mess up for the race, you want to have points,” he added.

“Somehow, I was like really, [feeling] okay. I didn't feel anything, that much, of pressure.”

Tsunoda finished 11th in Zandvoort, one place ahead of his team mate. But he thenfinished 10th at Monza to pick up a point for the team and help them in their fight against Alpine.

“The feeling I had, crossing the line, finishing P10, is definitely a bit more special P10 than certainly last three years of my career. Felt like really similar feeling towards first time I scored points in AlphaTauri [in my] first year.

“I felt very valuable, [more] than usual. I was so happy, team are happy, and the kind of moments that you can celebrate with the team – that we had a good race weekend – is something I didn't have for a while. It was a very nice moment.”

As to Tsunoda’s future, he is still trying to secure a full-time drive for next season. But it is a tough ask, with very few open seats left available.

“My primary focus is F1. I'm trying to be back. That's my target and I'm not thinking anything else. For myself, it's fortunate that I got opportunities so I try and maximise it and hope I can be back in 2027.”

title: The power unit manufacturers with the most wins in F1 history
excerpt:
Ferrari may be the most iconic team in F1 history, with their scarlet liveries and roster of legendary drivers, but Mercedes drew alongside them at the top of the list of the most successful power unit manufacturers with Kimi Antonelli's win at the 2026 Spanish Grand Prix.

From these two motorsport powerhouses to defunct companies like Coventry Climax and BRM, here are the top 10 engine producers with the most Formula 1 wins over the last 76 years…

=1. Ferrari – 251 wins

Ferrari were part of the inaugural F1 season back in 1950 and haven’t missed a year since, enjoying vast success over the decades with drivers like Alberto Ascari, Niki Lauda and Michael Schumacher.

They’ve also managed to net a colossal 251 victories with their own engines in that time – Charles Leclerc celebrated the team’s 250th at the 2026 British Grand Prix, while the extra one came from Sebastian Vettel’s maiden win with Toro Rosso in 2008, when they were a customer of the Scuderia.

Taking it back even further, Ferrari’s very first Grand Prix triumph was thanks to Jose Froilan Gonzalez, otherwise known as the Pampas Bull. He joined the team for five rounds in 1951 and finished on the podium at every one, including taking the win at Silverstone.

=1. Mercedes – 251 wins

Mercedes only competed in two F1 campaigns (1954 and 1955) before taking a hefty sabbatical, returning in part as an engine supplier for Sauber and McLaren in the mid-1990s, with Brawn GP and Racing Point joining their customer list at a later date.

Their original stint produced two Drivers’ Championships for Juan Manuel Fangio, but their modern power unit achievements are largely down to McLaren’s Mika Hakkinen (1998 and 1999 World Champion), Brawn GP’s Jenson Button (2009 World Champion), and of course, Mercedes’ full re-entry to the sport in 2010.

Why Brawn GP’s fairy tale is the F1 story that keeps on giving

Although they came back to the sport as a constructor with Schumacher and Nico Rosberg, it took two years to win a race, and another two before they clinched their first title.

By that time, Lewis Hamilton had signed for the squad and went on to claim 85 of Mercedes’ total wins while Rosberg, Kimi Antonelli, Valtteri Bottas and George Russell have also contributed to the record.

3. Ford Cosworth – 176 wins

The Cosworth DFV was one of the most dominant engines ever seen in F1, delivering 155 wins across outfits like Team Lotus, Brabham, Tyrrell and Williams. If a squad didn’t make their own engine between the 1960s and 1980s, this was the one they were all desperate to use.

Jim Clark secured its first win at the 1967 Dutch Grand Prix, where he drove from P8 to P1 in the Lotus 49, but a greater indicator of its success was the fact that every single race in the 1969 and 1973 seasons was won by a DFV-powered car.

The shift into the turbo era forced Ford Cosworth to evolve, with later variants of the engine clinching an additional 21 wins. These were predominantly achieved by Benetton and McLaren, but Giancarlo Fisichella holds the honour of netting the final victory at the 2003 Brazilian Grand Prix with Jordan.

4. Renault – 169 wins

You can’t speak of turbocharged engines without mentioning Renault. They were the first to regularly use the invention, and after two seasons of agonisingly poor reliability – it took 14 races to log their first finish – 1979 produced the breakthrough they needed.

Jean-Pierre Jabouille, who had patiently endured every retirement to that point, won that year’s French Grand Prix, but it was Alain Prost’s arrival in 1981 that unlocked Renault’s potential. After three years and nine triumphs, they declined as a works team once he departed, leading to their eventual withdrawal in 1986.

Alonso’s first F1 title win with Renault remembered

Ironically, they accomplished more when turbocharged engines were banned in 1989, when they began to supply Williams. Further collaborations with Benetton and Red Bull increased their number of wins to 169 overall, with Esteban Ocon taking their final one at the 2021 Hungarian Grand Prix.

Renault once again departed F1 at the end of the 2025 season, leading Alpine to switch from the French manufacturer to Mercedes under the new-for-2026 regulations.

5. Honda – 89 wins

Like Renault, Honda have had a somewhat fractured presence in F1, with their first entry occurring in 1964. They found early success by building their own engine and chassis as Richie Ginter reached the top step at the 1965 Mexican Grand Prix.

The company’s focus moved to road cars before they came back as a supplier for Spirit, Williams, Lotus, McLaren and Tyrrell at various times between 1983 and 1992. Not every team received the same level of factory support, but Nigel Mansell, Nelson Piquet, Ayrton Senna and Prost all proved that Honda could provide an unbeatable engine.

However, they pulled out again due to financial reasons before eventually purchasing BAR, which became Brawn GP when Honda suddenly exited again amid the 2008 economic crisis. Finally, they enjoyed a fruitful partnership with Red Bull from 2019 onwards, and Max Verstappen gave them their first win in the V6 turbo-hybrid era.

Their total ultimately reached 89 victories over four separate stints, with the 2021 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix marking their last, but that was far from the end of Honda’s time in F1 – more on that later.

6. Coventry Climax – 40 wins

Coventry Climax had manufactured engines since the turn of the 20th century, but it wasn’t until the 1950s that they began to appear in racing cars. Although Stirling Moss scored their first win at the 1958 Argentine Grand Prix, it was clear that their standard 2-litre engine wasn’t powerful enough to regularly compete with their rivals.

Things changed in 1959, when a 2.5-litre version took Jack Brabham to World Championship glory. The engine was also valuable in Lotus, Cooper, Brabham, and Lola chassis as it won 40 Grands Prix between 1958 and 1965.

It bowed out in style as Clark secured the 1965 title with his third and final career Grand Slam at the German Grand Prix, with Coventry Climax leaving the motorsport world when the 3-litre formula was introduced.

Five current drivers compared to past F1 stars

7. Honda RBPT – 38 wins

Verstappen’s hard-fought 2021 drivers’ title also marked Honda’s departure from F1, but they continued to help his team transition to their own in-house engine production named Red Bull Powertrains (RBPT).

As such, a new agreement was signed that saw the team take over the Honda engine IP to the end of the 2025 season, with the company providing support when required. This led to one of the most dominant years of recent memory as Red Bull won all bar one race in 2023, with the team scoring 860 points.

2024 and 2025 weren’t quite as productive, but they nevertheless ended with 38 victories overall to take seventh on the list.

8. TAG Porsche – 25 wins

Short-lived but immensely successful, this engine was used by McLaren between 1983 and 1987. Built by Porsche and funded by TAG, it was originally planned to debut in 1984, but Lauda insisted that they should test it beforehand and so the car was modified to accommodate the engine for the Dutch Grand Prix.

It was effective almost immediately and Prost made the most of it to win the season-opening 1984 Brazilian Grand Prix, though it was his team mate Lauda who would be crowned that season’s champion.

Between them, they netted 25 victories with the engine before McLaren changed their allegiance to Honda in 1988, inspired by the strong performances the Japanese company had logged with Williams.

9. BMW – 20 wins

The early years of F1 featured on-and-off private entries with BMW backing, but it was in the 1980s when the German manufacturer fully committed to the sport, deciding to directly challenge Renault’s turbo engines with their own version.

While they initially negotiated an exclusive deal with Brabham, the team opted to rely on Cosworth-powered cars, straining the fledgling relationship. Team Principal Bernie Ecclestone was convinced to give them a chance that paid off at the 1982 Canadian Grand Prix, won by Piquet.

More triumphs followed, but the ban on turbocharged engines for 1989 brought a temporary end to BMW’s involvement. They went on to take Renault’s place in a deal with Williams and delivered a competitive engine for the 2000 season, with a more aggressive evolution securing victory at the 2001 San Marino Grand Prix.

By 2003, Williams could consistently fight for wins but weren’t able to match Schumacher’s dominance with Ferrari, resulting in the end of the partnership in 2005.

BMW’s subsequent purchase of Sauber was a less successful venture – they only claimed one win, with Robert Kubica at the 2008 Canadian Grand Prix, and decided to sell the team back to Peter Sauber.

10. BRM – 18 wins

British Racing Motors, also known as BRM, got off to a shaky start in F1 as their overly ambitious engines didn’t generate the results they were hoping for. However, after some delayed development, Jo Bonnier claimed their first win at the 1959 Dutch Grand Prix to provide a much-needed boost.

Alfred Owen, a partner in the company, threatened to cancel the entire project if they didn’t start to achieve more, and chose to promote former Rolls-Royce employee Tony Rudd to the role of Chief Development Engineer. This proved to be a stroke of genius as he fixed basic problems that had plagued the team for years, culminating in Graham Hill’s triumph in the 1962 Drivers’ Championship.

BRM also began to sell engines to privateers, but their performances turned lacklustre and they left F1 in 1977 with 18 Grand Prix victories – 17 as a works team, and one under Team Lotus.

title: Alpine announce Mike Elliott as Chief Technical Officer
excerpt:
Alpine have announced that Mike Elliott is joining the team as Chief Technical Officer, marking his return to Formula 1 after leaving Mercedes towards the end of the 2023 season.

Elliott brings a wealth of experience to the position, having worked in the sport across 23 years since first becoming an aerodynamicist for McLaren back in 2000.

He went on to progress to other roles within the team before moving to Renault in 2008, remaining with the Enstone-based outfit until 2012 when he joined Mercedes.

After taking on the position of Head of Aerodynamics, the Briton would later become Technology Director from 2017 to 2021 and then Technical Director between 2021 and 2023.

He subsequently swapped roles with James Allison in 2023 to become Chief Technical Officer, before his departure was announced six months later.

In a statement confirming his appointment at Alpine, the team stated that Elliott will “oversee the technical and engineering functions at the team's factory at Enstone” in his new position, adding: “He has a proven track record in the sport, having contributed to an impressive eight Constructors' and eight Drivers' Championships.

“Elliott's arrival at Enstone strengthens the team's technical capabilities as the team looks to build on the improved performances on track and close the gap to the top four teams.”

title: Red Bull shine light on 'very different picture' of Liam Lawson
excerpt:
Amazing what a difference time and experience make, with Liam Lawson proving a point.

Laurent Mekies has declared that Liam Lawson's recent run of three races back at Red Bull has presented "a very different picture" from the driver's brief and turbulent spell at the team last year.

Racing Bulls driver Lawson was asked to step back into the senior Red Bull seat as cover for Isack Hadjar after the Frenchman suffered a wrist injury over the summer break.

The 24-year-old New Zealander initially finished seventh in the Netherlands, followed by P14 in Italy after contact with Audi's Nico Hülkenberg damaged his front wing, before delivering a sixth-place finish in Spain last time out.

That form stands in sharp contrast to the two races Lawson endured as Max Verstappen's team-mate at the start last year, leading to him being demoted back to Racing Bulls in favour of Yuki Tsunoda.

Speaking after the Spanish Grand Prix in Madrid, Mekies gave Lawson credit for adapting quickly to unfamiliar machinery.

"He's done a very good job," said Mekies, speaking to the media, including RacingNews365.

"We all know how difficult it is to jump to a different team, to a different car, and I think he has done that to the best of our expectations."

Referencing the "very important points" collected by Lawson in Madrid and Zandvoort, he added: "It's a very different picture compared to the first two races of 2025 when he was in the team, so we are thankful and happy with that."

Lawson 'very, very strong'

Asked about Lawson's growth as a driver, Mekies pointed to a calmer, more focused approach behind the wheel.

"He has continued to grow as a driver," he said. "He's very calm in the car, he's very focused.

"I don't know if he's making an effort or not, but he's certainly managed to keep things simple in the way he tracks with the team and in the way he tackles his own performance and the car performance.

"So he's focused on the essentials, trying to get the basics right, and it's working for him.

"Of course, with more time in the car, you can then get to another degree of finesse, maybe. But up to this point, he's been very, very strong."

title: Colton Herta makes racing career declaration as F1 hopes fade
excerpt:
Colton Herta moved over to European racing this year in the hope of obtaining an F1 seat in the near future.

Colton Herta has insisted he will not partake in a second season of Formula 2 next year.

The nine-time IndyCar race winner made the switch to the junior category this season with Hitech, while also carrying out development driver duties for the new Cadillac F1 team.

Cadillac has highlighted its desire to field an American driver in the near future, with Herta deemed a potential option by the team.

It has put a major hurdle in his pursuit of an F1 drive and has led to speculation that he could opt to return to the United States in 2027.

Herta vows to remain a fan of F2

title: Arvid Lindblad fires staunch F1 defence: 'I'm allowed to crash'
excerpt:
Arvid Lindblad has defended his practice crash at F1's recent Spanish Grand Prix, insisting that as a rookie, he is "allowed to make" such mistakes.

The Racing Bulls driver crashed at Turn 13 during second practice at Madrid, having set the fourth-fastest time in the session, before going onto qualify in 10th place - his 10th Q3 appearance in 14 races.

In the race, Lindblad finished in ninth for his ninth points finish of his rookie season, and his eighth in the last nine races, since a DNS in Canada.

His best result has been sixth in Monaco in a strong season for Racing Bulls, as the Briton defended his right to make mistakes such as the FP2 shunt in Madrid, which impacted the right-hand side of the car.

"I lost a lot of confidence, which is so important on a street track, missed basically all of FP3, and wasn't happy in qualifying, but I managed to put a lap together and put it in Q3," Lindblad told media, including RacingNews365.

"I definitely think that if I hadn't had the crash, the trajectory to qualifying would have been very different, and I would have been a lot happier.

"It is something to learn from, and in the end, I am not going to beat myself up for crashing because it is something that is inevitable.

"I've been so on the limit this year, I've been so fast, and it was my 10th Q3 [appearance] of the season.

"I am allowed to make mistakes, and I am going to learn from it."

The article continues below.

Lindblad's bouncing back

As he impresses in his rookie season, Lindblad also pointed to the fact that he felt he had shown he was able to overcome adversity when it struck.

"I think it is good, and that I've shown again, and I've shown all year, that when things get difficult, I can still bounce back," he continued.

"[It was] in Japan, there was an issue in Budapest and the same [in Madrid], this time it was a bit more of my own fault, but I am happy with how we bounced back. It wasn't easy."

title: Madrid F1 track designer responds to heavy criticism after woeful F1 debut
excerpt:
Jarno Zaffelli, CEO of the company behind the design of the Madring F1 track, has admitted that only “minimal” changes are possible to the layout going forward.

The circuit made its F1 debut last weekend as it took over as the host of the Spanish Grand Prix.

However, it produced a largely uninteresting race, with the support categories also seeing a lack of overtaking action throughout the weekend.

The track has received criticism from fans in the aftermath, with some calling for change to improve the show next time around.

But as Zaffelli explained, environmental constraints make such proposals difficult.

"Some changes are possible, but they are minimal,” Zaffelli told motorsport.com.

“From what has been publicly stated, some of the options discussed seem to be closer to intentions that were already present in our original project, which included an overtaking opportunity at Turn 5.”

[Article continues below]

Zaffelli denies 'blank sheet' starting point

Explaining what was supposed to be different about Turn 5, which is one of the tightest points on the track, Zaffelli said: “Turn 5 was supposed to be tighter and have less cornering.

“And in our design, inside Turn 6 there wasn't an asphalt run-off area, but a gravel solution, to force the drivers to take a slower route and avoid going straight because it would have penalised their lap time.

“The logic of the sequence wasn't to gain time through banking, but to create two trajectories with opposing advantages.”

Madrid has signed up with F1 for the long-term, with a 10-year deal in place.

Amid the criticism, Zaffelli has denied that the process of starting the layout of the track began from a blank sheet of paper, insisting it could only work around the restrictions of the land available.

"What was described as a blank sheet of paper is actually a highly urbanised area with precise constraints for designing a circuit suitable for Formula 1,” he said.

“A detailed map reveals that the layout faced very stringent constraints in many places, as new exhibition halls had already been designed and approved by urban planning authorities, just as the road network had already been planned along predefined lines.

“This is precisely why a great deal of creativity was required: the constraints limited the scope of the design, but they didn't determine a single solution.

“We had to invent geometries, sequences, and trajectories capable of generating a circuit with its own identity within those structural limitations and the constraints dictated by FIA safety regulations.”

title: Kimi Antonelli addresses possibility of future Ferrari F1 move
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli says he "doesn't rule out" one day joining Ferrari - but that he wants to "win as much as possible" with Mercedes.

Antonelli is closing in on becoming the youngest F1 champion with an 81-point lead over team-mate George Russell, and eight grand prix wins to Russell's two.

He would shatter Sebastian Vettel's record of youngest champion by over three years, with the Italian the first to be crowned champion since Alberto Ascari in 1953.

The last Italian to race full-time for Ferrari was Michele Alboreto in 1985, with Ivan Capelli, Nicola Larini, Luca Badoer, and Giancarlo Fisichella all making substitute appearances since.

However, whilst 20-year-old Antonelli does not one day rule joining the Scuderia, he has explained why he "owes a debt" to Mercedes.

"Now I'm fine where I am," Antonelli told Automoto Italy when asked about a potential future move to Ferrari.

"I am very happy to be at Mercedes, also because I feel I owe them a debt for all the opportunities they have given me.

"They were the ones who believed in me when I was only 12 years old. They have accompanied me on this path of growth, and I hope to reap many successes with them in the future.

"Then we'll see. I don't rule anything out, but today the goal is to win as much as possible with Mercedes."

The article continues below.

Antonelli's Monza reaction

At the recent Italian Grand Prix, Antonelli won from 19th on the grid, the first driver to do so since Bill Vukovich at the 1954 Indy 500.

Only John Watson at the 1983 USA West Grand Prix has won from further back, doing so from 22nd, with Antonelli also the first Italian to win his home race since Ludovico Scarfiotti in 1966.

Reflecting on that weekend, Antonelli spoke of the "goosebumps" he received on the podium.

"The charge of the fans during the GP was incredible," he said.

"It gave me the push to try to do even better. The podium in Monza is the most beautiful of the year, and hearing everyone sing the anthem in unison and shout my name gave me goosebumps."

title: Inside Red Bull's season rise: two major upgrades but two big problems remain
excerpt:
From a mid-pack position to competing for victories: Red Bull’s tremendous progress in 2026 is evident in the numbers.

Red Bull's progress across the course of this F1 season so far tells a clear story. A car that was nowhere near competitive in March has become one that finished just 4.3 seconds off the win in Madrid at the weekend.

Comparing the results from Melbourne through to Spain shows a team that has clawed its way forward, even if plenty of issues remain unresolved.

The opening weeks of the campaign were downright difficult for the Milton Keynes-based team. Max Verstappen crossed the line in sixth place in Australia after a qualifying crash left him to fight through from the back.

Not a disaster, particularly given it was the team's first season running an in-house power unit, but not the kind of result Red Bull was prepared to accept either.

The RB22 lacked outright pace, and the team battled with the car sitting above the minimum weight limit of 768 kilograms.

China and Japan did nothing to reverse the trend. Verstappen and Isack Hadjar were both stuck in the midfield and hit by reliability problems on top of it.

Verstappen retired from the Chinese Grand Prix in Shanghai, and the starts across both weekends were downright difficult.

See below for Red Bull’s average lap gap to winner Kimi Antonelli in Japan. Note: Verstappen frequently battled with Pierre Gasly.

The Miami turning point

The team's first real step forward arrived in Miami, where a substantial upgrade package was introduced. It included a rotating rear wing, quickly nicknamed the 'Macarena wing' in the paddock, revised sidepods, a modified steering column following complaints from Verstappen, and a weight saving of roughly six kilograms.

The impact was immediate. Verstappen qualified on the front row in Miami and finished fifth, his best showing of the year to that point.

That rear wing, however, later created a headache. A fault in its locking mechanism, which stopped the airflow from recovering in time under braking, triggering a sudden loss of rear-end downforce, caused problems at both the Red Bull Ring and Silverstone.

Red Bull reverted to a conventional rear wing for Spa while its engineers reinforced the actuator at the factory. The updated version has run without issue since.

A second significant upgrade landed in Austria, covering changes to the sidepod inlets and engine cover cooling alongside further weight reduction.

Verstappen immediately banked P2 at the Red Bull Ring, one and a half seconds behind George Russell. It stands as his best result of the season alongside Madrid.

Driver

Max Verstappen

Dutch

3

Problems for Red Bull to solve

It has been a rapid rise, but neither Verstappen nor Red Bull will be satisfied yet. The team currently sits, on average, as the fourth-strongest outfit on the grid. Closing that gap for good means fixing two persistent problems.

The first is energy management. Under the 2026 power unit regulations, which have removed the MGU-H and given the electric MGU-K 350kW, nearly half of total output, more energy needs recovering than is available in a normal braking zone.

That produces what is known in the sport as 'superclipping': the battery runs dry before the end of straights, forcing the MGU-K to stop delivering power so it can recharge.

Mercedes handles this far better than Red Bull, as was clear at Monza, where Verstappen could only keep pace while tucked in the slipstream of Kimi Antonelli and Russell before dropping back on his own.

The second issue may be even more fundamental. Red Bull refers to it internally as car degradation, not ordinary tyre wear but a loss of mechanical and aerodynamic balance over the course of a session or race. The RB22 performs at its best with a full fuel tank.

As fuel weight decreases, the car becomes relatively weaker rather than stronger, exactly where teams normally expect improvement. Rear-end instability increases and the tyres overheat quickly.

It is the opposite of how a race car should behave, and it is a problem Red Bull has been wrestling with for years.

In conclusion, there remains plenty of work to secure regular victories, but the progress made since the season opener leaves Verstappen and Red Bull firmly on the right trajectory.

title: Will charm offensive keep Fernando Alonso in F1?
excerpt:
Fernando Alonso’s F1 future remains uncertain. But why did FIA President Mohammed Ben Sulayem offer him a helping hand?

Formula 1 is not ready to let Fernando Alonso slip away just yet.

FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem recently indicated that he is examining adjustments to help engine manufacturers who are falling behind, such as Honda, in a bid to stop the two-time F1 champion from walking away prematurely because his Aston Martin machinery cannot compete at the front.

Ben Sulayem made his position clear at the New Economy Forum in Madrid, over the Spanish Grand Prix weekend, making clear that it would be unacceptable for a driver of Alonso's stature to leave the sport simply because his car is not capable of fighting at the sharp end.

It remains unclear exactly what measure the FIA president has in mind. What is certain is that the ADUO [Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities] mechanism is part of the discussion.

The system allows engine manufacturers who are lagging behind, such as Honda, to receive extra development resources to close the gap to the benchmark supplier. Red Bull is currently regarded as the strongest of the manufacturers.

[Article continues below]

Driver

Fernando Alonso

Spanish

14

Quit or keep going?

The motive behind the FIA's interest is obvious. Alonso has been openly questioning his future beyond 2027, driven by Aston Martin's disappointing form and his own criticism of the current regulations.

The Spaniard has repeatedly hit out at the outsized role of electric power management in the current generation of engines, arguing that driver skill has become too subordinate to the battery as a result.

Before the Spanish Grand Prix, Ben Sulayem had already spoken with Aston Martin owner Lawrence Stroll and indicated he intended to speak personally with Alonso to try to persuade him to extend his career in the top flight.

Alonso himself says he is in regular contact with both Ben Sulayem and F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali, and has stated that his decision for 2027 will depend partly on whether the technical regulations again reward driving talent more heavily.

Rule changes aimed at limiting the influence of the battery have already been announced.

The text continues below the image.

© XPBimages

Aston Martin's rivals were not particularly taken aback by Ben Sulayem's comments. Racing Bulls team principal Laurent Mekies said: "As much as we don't always agree with each other, I think that as a sport we try to approach the regulations with a reasonably open mind.

"And you may recall that earlier this year, an initial change was already made to the ADUO regulations, precisely to help the teams that were falling far further behind than initially estimated. All teams voted on this, and we voted in favour of the change, in the best interest of the sport."

"So, as I said: we don't agree on everything, but as stakeholders within the sport, we normally find solutions when there's a situation that needs to be resolved or requires support."

Aston Martin itself is working the problem from more than one angle. Alongside a race seat, the Silverstone-based outfit has also offered Alonso a role beyond the cockpit, including a multi-year ambassadorship and an advisory position within the organisation for life after his active career.

A tilt at the 24 Hours of Le Mans in the Aston Martin Valkyrie is also on the table, a distinct possibility for next season as next year's race does not clash with a grand prix.

Whether Alonso will still be racing in F1 beyond 2026 remains an open question. But the sport's charm offensive to keep him there is now in full swing.

title: Cadillac F1 owner facing major lawsuit over fraud allegations
excerpt:
Mark Walter, owner of TWG Global and majority stakeholder in the Cadillac Formula 1 Team, is facing a proposed class-action lawsuit alleging fraudulent concealment, breach of contract, aiding and abetting fraud, and civil conspiracy, among other claims.

The suit, filed in the Southern District of Florida by law firm Robbins Geller Rudman & Dowd on behalf of 67-year-old Miami resident Ira Rosner, centres on an annuity purchased through Delaware Life Insurance Company. Delaware Life, Group 1001, TWG Global, and Guggenheim Partners are all named as defendants alongside Walter.

According to USA Today, the complaint alleges that Walter and the named companies conducted a "systematic scheme to conceal and misrepresent the allocation of insurer assets in entities affiliated with or controlled by Walter."

At the heart of the claim is the allegation that Group 1001, Walter's Indiana-based parent company, deliberately withheld grand jury subpoenas received by Delaware Life in February until a compulsory regulatory disclosure in June.

The lawsuit further alleges that only around 3% of Delaware Life's invested assets were disclosed as related-party investments, "when in truth the figure was more than 1,000% greater."

Walter's TWG Global has become an increasingly prominent force in motorsport through TWG Motorsports, the division behind the Cadillac Formula 1 Team.

Cadillac entered F1 as the grid's 11th constructor in 2026 through a partnership between TWG Motorsports and General Motors, with Walter holding a majority stake.

The team is contesting its debut season with Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas as race drivers, Zhou Guanyu as reserve, and Colton Herta in a test role.

Marcin Budkowski serves as team principal, overseeing day-to-day racing operations after taking over from Graeme Lowdon last month.

TWG Motorsports has publicly stated that the Cadillac F1 team is not for sale and that it has no intention of exiting its stake, despite speculation prompted by the legal and regulatory scrutiny surrounding Walter personally.

title: F1 drivers engaged in 'mental warfare' as 'physical combat' skill declines
excerpt:
Alex Albon believes F1 drivers are now more engaged in "mental warfare" rather than "physical combat" during grands prix.

The new energy management demands in 2026 have brought about a huge change in how drivers go about wheel-to-wheel racing and setting up overtakes, as deploying their battery to pass a rival means they will be immediately re-passed in what is known as 'yo-yo racing.'

This is only a concern on 'energy-starved' tracks such as Australia's Albert Park, Japan's Suzuka, Britain's Silverstone, Belgium's Spa or Italy's Monza, whilst other circuits such as Monaco, the Hungaroring in Hungary and the Netherlands' Zandvoort are known as 'energy-rich' meaning cars can continually harvest energy to deploy.

In pre-season, the new demands were likened to a high-speed game of chess, with Williams racer Albon going further and explaining how drivers can no longer play certain "games" with rivals.

"I think the mental warfare has overtaken the physical combat in the sense that it is now very much about the [energy] management," Albon told media, including RacingNews365.

"I think it is more tactical. There is an element of tactics where last year, you could only play DRS games, like trying to back off and get a car to go in front of you on the DRS line.

"There were still anti-overtaking things that you could do, but this is more like GPS data analysis going on at the factory giving us immediate response times of what we can do and what mode switches we need to change to anticipate what cars are doing around us.

"In many ways, it is tactical, but at the same time, sometimes, we feel helpless, like you just cannot defend anymore."

The article continues below.

Albon on a lack of 'defensive skills'

The Thai also expanded on how the rules were restricting the ability of the drivers to show off their defensive skills when in battle.

"There are no real defensive skills because the overtake is such an overrun," he said.

"I feel like we've missed a bit of the you've got to overtake on the brakes, you've got to get the car offline, get clean air, get dirty air, and I miss that.

"But in terms of the tactics, I've spent a lot more time speaking with HPP this year than I did last year."

title: Remarkable Ollie Millroy interview following horrific crash and dramatic rescue
excerpt:
A week and a half after his heavy crash in the GT race at Shanghai International Circuit, Ollie Millroy speaks from his hospital bed. His Ferrari caught fire, and Dutchman Loek Hartog stopped, climbed out and pulled him from the flames.

Millroy came away with six broken ribs, a broken collarbone, a broken hand and a punctured lung. What he doesn't have is a memory of it. Post-traumatic amnesia has wiped everything from 30 seconds before the impact to an hour afterwards. He only found out what had happened when Loek came to see him in hospital that evening.

In this conversation he talks about that strange blank in his head, about what you say to the man who saved your life, about his young son seeing the crash on YouTube, and about why it isn't the impact that frightens him most, but what didn't happen afterwards. Together with Hartog he wants to use the attention around their story to push for better safety in motorsport.

title: FIA issue statement after reports of WEC promoter rift emerge
excerpt:
The FIA has issued a statement clarifying that its contract with the Automobile Club de l'Ouest for the promotion of the World Endurance Championship remains "in place until the end of 2027."

A report was published on Thursday from respected German publication Auto Motor Und Sport stating that a contract for the promotion of the WEC was not in place for 2027, and that a public tender could be opened.

This would have meant that the Le Mans 24 Hours would not have been on the calendar with a new promoter, as that race is owned and run by the ACO.

The governing body has now rejected that claim and has clarified that the WEC will be promoted by the ACO in 2027, whilst a new contract is agreed for 2028 and beyond.

It is also understood by RacingNews365 that there were inconsistencies within the original AMUS report.

"The FIA World Endurance Championship has enjoyed sustained growth since the introduction of the Hypercar and LMGT3 regulations, competing this season across seven countries," began the statement, issued to RacingNews365.

"This achievement is the result of extensive collaboration between drivers, teams, manufacturers, the FIA, the promoter, the ACO and the millions of fans who follow the championship.

"The FIA and ACO are continuing discussions regarding an extension of the promoter agreement. The current agreement with ACO remains in place until the end of 2027."

title: Lewis Hamilton handed 'truly remarkable' verdict as key question posed
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has enjoyed a more positive outing with Ferrari this year after a challenging opening campaign with the team.

Former F1 driver David Coulthard has stated he finds it “truly remarkable” that Lewis Hamilton still has a desire to compete in the sport.

title: Ferrari detail huge scale to overcome F1 rival advantage
excerpt:
Ferrari has continuously voiced its concern with its straight-line speed this year.

Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur has outlined the scale of the challenge his squad faces in closing the straight-line speed gap.

Throughout the 2026 campaign, the Italian squad has noted that it is lacking pace at top speed compared to the likes of Mercedes.

Lewis Hamilton reiterated the point at the recent Italian Grand Prix, despite the team introducing a fresh engine upgrade.

However, Vasseur insisted the situation is vastly complicated, and the push to develop an upgraded engine is a much bigger task compared to the aero.

“The process of the engine is mega long,” Vasseur told media including RacingNews365.

“The chassis, you can make an upgrade from one day to the other very quickly and come back into the pace," said Vasseur.

"On the engine, the process is mega long because the lead time of the parts is long and the cost cap is not easy - you have to produce the engine for the season.

"And if you want to start to do the development, you have to produce a new batch of engines.”

[Article continues below]

Ferrari concede ADUO help can't overcome defecit

This year, the FIA introduced the ADUO (Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities) to give those struggling an extra boost to make up the margin.

However, Vasseur insisted that the helping hand from the programme is not enough to get it back on even terms with the benchmark.

“We are not expecting to recover with ADUO 1 or ADUO 2,” he said. “We are doing small steps.

"If you make a small step on the engine, keep in mind that behind us, it was hundredths of a second.

“In terms of position, even if you make a couple of horsepower, it's a good step on the grid.

“Now we will have a new engine next year. For sure, the target is to catch up as soon as possible."
